errors.title: Present perfect for duration
errors.what: using the present simple or continuous for something that started in the past and continues ('I live here since 2019', 'I am working here for five years')
errors.summary: This error often persists because the meaning is usually clear, even if the grammar is imprecise. However, it can make your English sound less natural and occasionally lead to subtle misunderstandings about duration.
errors.listenFor: Pay attention when you describe an action or state that began at a specific point in the past and is still ongoing in the present.

contrasts.wrong: I live here since 2019.
contrasts.right: I have lived here since 2019.
contrasts.note: Use present perfect for actions or states that started in the past and continue now.

contrasts.wrong: She is working on this project for three months.
contrasts.right: She has been working on this project for three months.
contrasts.note: Present perfect continuous emphasizes the ongoing nature and duration of an activity.

contrasts.wrong: They know each other for a long time.
contrasts.right: They have known each other for a long time.
contrasts.note: Stative verbs like 'know' use the present perfect, not continuous, for duration.

contrasts.wrong: He studies English since he was a child.
contrasts.right: He has studied English since he was a child.
contrasts.note: The action of studying began in the past and continues up to the present moment.

contrasts.wrong: We are waiting for the results for hours.
contrasts.right: We have been waiting for the results for hours.
contrasts.note: Use present perfect continuous for an activity that has been ongoing for a period.

contrasts.wrong: The company exists for over fifty years.
contrasts.right: The company has existed for over fifty years.
contrasts.note: 'Exist' is a stative verb; use present perfect to express its duration.

errors.title: Present perfect or past simple
errors.what: using the present perfect with a finished time ('I have seen him yesterday') or the past simple for life experience and recent news
errors.summary: This error persists because the distinction between finished and unfinished time can be subtle, especially when the past event has present relevance. It can lead to misunderstandings about the recency or ongoing nature of information.
errors.listenFor: Pay attention to whether you are discussing a specific past event or an experience relevant to the present moment.

contrasts.wrong: I have seen that documentary last night.
contrasts.right: I saw that documentary last night.
contrasts.note: A specific past time adverbial requires the past simple.

contrasts.wrong: We lived in this neighborhood since 2015.
contrasts.right: We have lived in this neighborhood since 2015.
contrasts.note: Duration continuing to the present uses the present perfect.

contrasts.wrong: I have visited Berlin in 2019 for a conference.
contrasts.right: I visited Berlin in 2019 for a conference.
contrasts.note: A specific past year requires the past simple.

errors.title: Articles with general and abstract nouns
errors.what: adding 'the' to general statements ('The life is hard', 'I like the music') or dropping 'a/the' with singular countable nouns ('She is engineer')
errors.summary: Article usage is highly idiomatic, making it a persistent challenge even for advanced speakers. Inaccurate article use can subtly undermine fluency and make speech sound less natural.
errors.listenFor: Notice if you add 'the' before general concepts or omit 'a' or 'the' before singular countable nouns.

contrasts.wrong: The life in the city is often very demanding.
contrasts.right: Life in the city is often very demanding.
contrasts.note: 'Life' in general does not take 'the'.

contrasts.wrong: I find the happiness in simple daily routines.
contrasts.right: I find happiness in simple daily routines.
contrasts.note: 'Happiness' as a general concept does not take 'the'.

contrasts.wrong: The knowledge is power in today's economy.
contrasts.right: Knowledge is power in today's economy.
contrasts.note: 'Knowledge' as an abstract concept does not take 'the'.

contrasts.wrong: She is experienced architect with a strong portfolio.
contrasts.right: She is an experienced architect with a strong portfolio.
contrasts.note: 'Architect' is a singular countable noun requiring 'a'.

contrasts.wrong: We need to find solution to this complex problem.
contrasts.right: We need to find a solution to this complex problem.
contrasts.note: 'Solution' is a singular countable noun requiring 'a'.

contrasts.wrong: He presented very compelling argument during the debate.
contrasts.right: He presented a very compelling argument during the debate.
contrasts.note: 'Argument' is a singular countable noun requiring 'a'.

errors.title: Uncountable nouns
errors.what: pluralising or counting uncountable nouns ('informations', 'advices', 'a feedback', 'researches', 'equipments')
errors.summary: This error often persists because many languages treat these nouns as countable, making the distinction subtle for advanced learners. It can make speech sound less natural and occasionally obscure the intended meaning.
errors.listenFor: Notice if you are adding an 's' or using 'a/an' before common uncountable nouns like 'information', 'advice', 'feedback', 'research', or 'equipment'.

contrasts.wrong: The team received several important informations regarding the project timeline.
contrasts.right: The team received several important pieces of information regarding the project timeline.
contrasts.note: Information is uncountable; use 'pieces of information' to quantify.

contrasts.wrong: I need some advices on how to manage my finances more effectively.
contrasts.right: I need some advice on how to manage my finances more effectively.
contrasts.note: Advice is uncountable; do not pluralize with 's'.

contrasts.wrong: We received a valuable feedback from the client after the presentation.
contrasts.right: We received valuable feedback from the client after the presentation.
contrasts.note: Feedback is uncountable; do not use 'a' before it.

contrasts.wrong: Her latest researches have significantly advanced the field of neuroscience.
contrasts.right: Her latest research has significantly advanced the field of neuroscience.
contrasts.note: Research is uncountable; do not pluralize with 's'.

contrasts.wrong: The laboratory requires new equipments to conduct the advanced experiments.
contrasts.right: The laboratory requires new equipment to conduct the advanced experiments.
contrasts.note: Equipment is uncountable; do not pluralize with 's'.

contrasts.wrong: They purchased many new furnitures for their renovated office space.
contrasts.right: They purchased many new pieces of furniture for their renovated office space.
contrasts.note: Furniture is uncountable; use 'pieces of furniture' to quantify.

errors.title: Word order in indirect questions
errors.what: keeping question order inside indirect questions ('Can you tell me where is the station?', 'I wonder what does it mean')
errors.summary: This error persists because it's a subtle grammatical point often missed in advanced learning. It makes speech sound less natural and can subtly impede clarity, despite overall fluency.
errors.listenFor: Listen for instances where you invert the subject and verb within a question embedded in another statement or question.

contrasts.wrong: Could you explain how does this system work?
contrasts.right: Could you explain how this system works?
contrasts.note: In indirect questions, use statement word order (subject-verb) after the question word.

contrasts.wrong: I'm not sure what is the best approach for this project.
contrasts.right: I'm not sure what the best approach for this project is.
contrasts.note: Maintain subject-verb order; the verb 'is' follows the subject 'the best approach'.

contrasts.wrong: Do you know when does the next flight depart?
contrasts.right: Do you know when the next flight departs?
contrasts.note: Avoid auxiliary verbs like 'does' in indirect questions; use simple present tense.

contrasts.wrong: She asked me where did I find that information.
contrasts.right: She asked me where I found that information.
contrasts.note: In indirect questions, do not use 'did'; change the verb to past simple.

contrasts.wrong: We need to determine why is the budget overspent.
contrasts.right: We need to determine why the budget is overspent.
contrasts.note: The subject 'the budget' precedes the verb 'is' in the embedded clause.

contrasts.wrong: He wondered if is it possible to reschedule the meeting.
contrasts.right: He wondered if it is possible to reschedule the meeting.
contrasts.note: After 'if' or 'whether', use subject-verb order, not inverted.

errors.title: 'Will' in if- and time clauses
errors.what: putting 'will' or 'would' in the if-clause or time clause ('If it will rain, we stay inside', 'When I will arrive, I call you', 'If I would know')
errors.summary: This error persists because context often clarifies meaning, making it less noticeable. However, it subtly detracts from fluency and precision, signaling a non-native command of advanced English grammar.
errors.listenFor: Pay close attention to whether you use 'will' or 'would' immediately following conjunctions like 'if', 'when', 'as soon as', or 'until'.

contrasts.wrong: If it will rain tomorrow, we should reschedule the outdoor event.
contrasts.right: If it rains tomorrow, we should reschedule the outdoor event.

contrasts.wrong: When I will finish this report, I will send it to the team.
contrasts.right: When I finish this report, I will send it to the team.
contrasts.note: Use simple present in time clauses referring to the future.

contrasts.wrong: As soon as she will arrive, we can begin the presentation.
contrasts.right: As soon as she arrives, we can begin the presentation.
contrasts.note: Simple present for future actions in time clauses.

contrasts.wrong: If I would know the answer, I would certainly tell you.
contrasts.right: If I knew the answer, I would certainly tell you.
contrasts.note: Use simple past in the if-clause for hypothetical present conditions.

contrasts.wrong: Until the new policy will be implemented, we must follow the old guidelines.
contrasts.right: Until the new policy is implemented, we must follow the old guidelines.
contrasts.note: Simple present for future events in time clauses.

contrasts.wrong: I will inform you if there will be any changes to the schedule.
contrasts.right: I will inform you if there are any changes to the schedule.
contrasts.note: Simple present for future conditions in if-clauses.

errors.what: choosing the wrong pattern after common verbs ('I suggest to meet', 'We look forward to hear from you', 'avoid to say', 'used to working' for past habits)
errors.summary: This error persists because it rarely impedes understanding, allowing it to become deeply ingrained. However, it subtly detracts from the speaker's fluency and precision, making their English sound less natural.
errors.listenFor: Pay close attention to the form of the second verb when it directly follows another verb in your sentences.

contrasts.wrong: I suggest to meet early to discuss the project timeline.
contrasts.right: I suggest meeting early to discuss the project timeline.
contrasts.note: "Suggest" is followed by a gerund.

contrasts.wrong: We look forward to hear from you regarding the proposal.
contrasts.right: We look forward to hearing from you regarding the proposal.
contrasts.note: "Look forward to" is a phrasal verb followed by a gerund.

contrasts.wrong: It's best to avoid to say anything controversial during negotiations.
contrasts.right: It's best to avoid saying anything controversial during negotiations.
contrasts.note: "Avoid" is followed by a gerund.

contrasts.wrong: When I was younger, I used to working long hours without fatigue.
contrasts.right: When I was younger, I used to work long hours without fatigue.
contrasts.note: "Used to" for past habits is followed by the base form of the verb.

contrasts.wrong: After much deliberation, they decided going with the alternative plan.
contrasts.right: After much deliberation, they decided to go with the alternative plan.
contrasts.note: "Decide" is followed by an infinitive.

contrasts.wrong: Despite the tight deadline, we managed finishing the report on time.
contrasts.right: Despite the tight deadline, we managed to finish the report on time.
contrasts.note: "Manage" is followed by an infinitive.

errors.title: Dependent prepositions
errors.what: the wrong or an extra preposition with verbs and adjectives ('discuss about', 'depend of', 'married with', 'responsible of', 'explain me')

errors.listenFor: Actively notice the prepositions you use directly after verbs and adjectives; check if they align with standard English usage.

contrasts.wrong: We need to discuss about the budget implications.
contrasts.right: We need to discuss the budget implications.
contrasts.note: The verb 'discuss' is transitive and takes a direct object without a preposition.

contrasts.wrong: Our success will depend of market conditions.
contrasts.right: Our success will depend on market conditions.
contrasts.note: The verb 'depend' is always followed by the preposition 'on' or 'upon'.

contrasts.wrong: She is married with a prominent architect.
contrasts.right: She is married to a prominent architect.
contrasts.note: When referring to a spouse, the adjective 'married' is followed by 'to'.

contrasts.wrong: He is responsible of the entire project.
contrasts.right: He is responsible for the entire project.
contrasts.note: The adjective 'responsible' is always followed by the preposition 'for'.

contrasts.wrong: Could you explain me the new policy?
contrasts.right: Could you explain the new policy to me?
contrasts.note: When 'explain' has both a direct and indirect object, the indirect object uses 'to'.

contrasts.wrong: I always listen at classical music while working.
contrasts.right: I always listen to classical music while working.
contrasts.note: The verb 'listen' is always followed by the preposition 'to'.

errors.title: Despite, although and however
errors.what: mixing up concession linkers ('despite of', 'although the rain', 'however' used like 'but' mid-sentence)
errors.summary: These errors persist because the core meaning of concession is understood, but the grammatical structures differ. This leads to subtle imprecision, undermining the speaker's advanced command of English.
errors.listenFor: Pay attention to whether you are using a full clause after 'although', a noun phrase after 'despite', and correct punctuation with 'however'.

contrasts.wrong: Despite of the recent downturn, investments are stable.
contrasts.right: Despite the recent downturn, investments are stable.
contrasts.note: 'Despite' does not take 'of'.

contrasts.wrong: Although the challenging circumstances, they met the deadline.
contrasts.right: Although the circumstances were challenging, they met the deadline.
contrasts.note: 'Although' introduces a clause (subject + verb).

contrasts.wrong: The proposal was ambitious, however it gained approval.
contrasts.right: The proposal was ambitious; however, it gained approval.
contrasts.note: 'However' is a conjunctive adverb, requiring stronger punctuation like a semicolon.

contrasts.wrong: Despite of the fact that he disagreed, he supported the decision.
contrasts.right: Despite the fact that he disagreed, he supported the decision.
contrasts.note: 'Despite' does not take 'of', even with 'the fact that'.

contrasts.wrong: She felt exhausted, although her presentation was flawless.
contrasts.right: She felt exhausted; however, her presentation was flawless.
contrasts.note: 'Although' connects clauses within a sentence; 'however' shows contrast between sentences.

contrasts.wrong: Although the heavy rain, the outdoor concert proceeded.
contrasts.right: Although it rained heavily, the outdoor concert proceeded.
contrasts.note: 'Although' requires a clause (subject + verb).

errors.listenFor: Pay close attention to your verb choices when combining them with common nouns, especially for actions, decisions, and social events.

contrasts.wrong: I always make a photo of the sunset when I am on vacation.
contrasts.right: I always take a photo of the sunset when I am on vacation.

contrasts.wrong: It is important to learn from the mistakes we do.
contrasts.right: It is important to learn from the mistakes we make.

contrasts.wrong: Many people make sport to stay healthy and active.
contrasts.right: Many people do sport to stay healthy and active.
contrasts.note: Do sport or exercise is the correct verb for engaging in physical activity.

contrasts.wrong: We are planning to make a party for her birthday next month.
contrasts.right: We are planning to have a party for her birthday next month.
contrasts.note: Have a party or throw a party is used for hosting a social gathering.

contrasts.wrong: Could you please make me a favor and pick up the dry cleaning?
contrasts.right: Could you please do me a favor and pick up the dry cleaning?
contrasts.note: Do a favor is the correct idiom for performing a helpful act.

errors.title: False friends
errors.what: words that look like a word in another language but mean something else ('actual' for current, 'eventually' for possibly, 'sympathetic' for nice, 'propose' for suggest, 'control' for check)
errors.summary: False friends persist because their similarity to native language words makes them seem correct. This leads to subtle misunderstandings and can undermine the speaker's credibility in professional contexts.
errors.listenFor: Pay close attention to words that sound or look like terms in your native language but might carry different meanings in English.

contrasts.wrong: We will eventually go to the conference next year.

contrasts.note: "Eventually" means in the end; "possibly" means perhaps.

contrasts.wrong: My new colleague is very sympathetic.

contrasts.note: "Sympathetic" means showing understanding; "kind" means friendly or generous.

contrasts.wrong: Please control the documents before sending them.
contrasts.right: Please check the documents before sending them.
contrasts.note: "Control" means to direct or manage; "check" means to verify.

contrasts.wrong: He is very sensible to criticism.
contrasts.right: He is very sensitive to criticism.
contrasts.note: "Sensible" means practical or reasonable; "sensitive" means easily affected.

errors.title: Say, tell, explain and suggest
errors.what: the wrong pattern after reporting verbs ('He said me that', 'She told that she was late', 'Can you explain me', 'He suggested me to wait')
errors.summary: These errors persist due to L1 interference and overgeneralization of 'tell' patterns. They subtly disrupt natural English flow, making communication less precise and marking speech as non-native.
errors.listenFor: Pay close attention to the grammatical structures immediately following 'say,' 'tell,' 'explain,' and 'suggest' in your own speech.

contrasts.wrong: He said me that the meeting was postponed until next week.
contrasts.right: He said that the meeting was postponed until next week.
contrasts.note: 'Say' does not take a direct object pronoun before a 'that' clause.

contrasts.wrong: She told that she would be late for the presentation.
contrasts.right: She told us that she would be late for the presentation.
contrasts.note: 'Tell' usually requires an indirect object (person) before a 'that' clause.

contrasts.wrong: Could you explain me the new policy changes?
contrasts.right: Could you explain the new policy changes to me?
contrasts.note: 'Explain' takes a direct object (thing) then 'to' + indirect object (person).

contrasts.wrong: My manager suggested me to consider the alternative proposal.
contrasts.right: My manager suggested that I consider the alternative proposal.
contrasts.note: 'Suggest' uses a 'that' clause with a subjunctive or a gerund, not 'to' + infinitive.

contrasts.wrong: The client said me that the project timeline was too ambitious.
contrasts.right: The client said to me that the project timeline was too ambitious.
contrasts.note: 'Say' can take 'to' + indirect object, but not a direct object pronoun.

contrasts.wrong: Please explain me how this new software integrates with our existing systems.
contrasts.right: Please explain to me how this new software integrates with our existing systems.
contrasts.note: 'Explain' requires 'to' before the indirect object when followed by 'how' or 'what'.

errors.title: For, since, ago and during
errors.what: mixing up time words ('since three years', 'before two weeks' for 'two weeks ago', 'during three hours')
errors.summary: Advanced learners often translate time expressions directly, leading to subtle but persistent errors with 'for,' 'since,' 'ago,' and 'during.' This impacts precision and can subtly undermine the speaker's fluency and credibility.
errors.listenFor: Notice how you express durations, starting points, and past events; specifically, check your use of 'for,' 'since,' 'ago,' and 'during.'

contrasts.wrong: I've been working on this report since three hours.
contrasts.right: I've been working on this report for three hours.
contrasts.note: Use 'for' to express a duration; 'since' indicates a starting point in time.

contrasts.wrong: We finalized the contract before two weeks.
contrasts.right: We finalized the contract two weeks ago.
contrasts.note: 'Ago' correctly places an event in the past relative to the present moment.

contrasts.wrong: The system was offline during a long time.
contrasts.right: The system was offline for a long time.
contrasts.note: 'For' specifies the duration of an event; 'during' indicates when something happens.

contrasts.wrong: She hasn't visited us for last Christmas.
contrasts.right: She hasn't visited us since last Christmas.
contrasts.note: 'Since' marks the beginning of a period that continues to the present.

contrasts.wrong: He completed the task during an hour.
contrasts.right: He completed the task in an hour.
contrasts.note: 'In an hour' means it took one hour to complete. 'For an hour' also works for duration.

contrasts.wrong: The decision was made since a moment.
contrasts.right: The decision was made a moment ago.
contrasts.note: 'Ago' is used for a specific point in the past, not 'since' in this context.

errors.what: the same stress for noun and verb pairs ('a REcord' and 'to reCORD', 'an INcrease' and 'to inCREASE')
errors.summary: This error persists because many noun-verb pairs are spelled identically, making the subtle shift in stress easily overlooked. Misplacing stress can obscure meaning or make speech sound less natural, despite advanced fluency.
errors.listenFor: Notice if the primary stress in two-syllable words shifts when the word functions as a noun versus a verb.

errors.title: Sentence stress and rhythm
errors.what: stressing every word evenly instead of the content words, so speech sounds flat and hard to follow
errors.summary: Even stress often persists because it's a rhythmic rather than a lexical error, making it difficult to self-correct. This flatness can make speech sound unnatural and less engaging, potentially obscuring the speaker's intended emphasis.
errors.listenFor: Pay attention to whether every word in your sentences receives similar emphasis, rather than allowing key content words to stand out.

errors.title: Stress for contrast and focus
errors.what: not moving the main stress to the new or contrasted word ('I said TUESday, not Thursday'; 'It's not MY problem')
errors.summary: This subtle prosodic error often persists because it doesn't impede grammatical correctness, making it hard to self-correct. However, it can lead to misunderstandings, diminish the impact of your message, and make your speech sound less natural to native listeners.
errors.listenFor: Pay attention to whether the most important word in your sentence receives the primary stress, especially when correcting or contrasting information.

contrasts.note: Stress on 'call' clarifies the intended action.

errors.title: Intonation in questions and tags
errors.what: rising on every question, or not using a fall on question tags that ask for agreement ('It's cold, isn't it?')
errors.summary: This intonation error often persists because it doesn't impede comprehension, yet it can subtly convey uncertainty or a lack of conviction. It costs the speaker nuance and authority in their communication, potentially undermining their message.
errors.listenFor: Pay attention to whether your voice consistently rises at the end of all questions, especially tag questions seeking agreement.

errors.title: Linking and connected speech
errors.what: pronouncing every word separately instead of linking ('turn_it_off', 'an_apple', 'what do you' as 'whaddya' in casual speech)
errors.summary: Advanced learners often focus on articulating each word distinctly, overlooking the natural flow of connected speech. This can make communication sound less fluid and occasionally impede listener comprehension.
errors.listenFor: Pay attention to whether your words flow together smoothly or if there are noticeable pauses and breaks between them.
